newsitem.title: GERMANY: Eva Braun play panned by critics in Berlin.
newsitem.headline: Eva Braun play panned by critics in Berlin.

text.p: A much-touted play dramatising in shocking detail the intimate life of Eva Braun, Adolf Hitler's lover of 16 years, was panned on Sunday by critics who found the "girlfriend of a mass murderer" more banal than intriguing.

"Eva, Hitlers Geliebte" (Eva, Hitler's Mistress), which opened in Berlin on Friday to a sell-out audience, presents a controversially sympathetic portrait of Germany's "first lady" during the Nazi Third Reich.

The monologue, starring Corinna Harfouch, condenses the time between Hitler and Braun's wedding on the night of April 28, 1945, and their suicide together in his bunker two days later into a 90-minute one-woman show.

Depicting Eva as a petulant ingenue with dreams of acting in Hollywood, Harfouch recounts with girlish giggles Braun's first sexual encounter with "Wolf", as she calls Hitler, on a sofa in Munich, "where he later sat with Chamberlain".

"I wanted to portray her as human with all the weaknesses and dreams and moments of happiness that would make her more accessible than this image of a monster by the side of a super-monster," said playwright Stefan Kolditz.

"Every person who comes knows that there was an Auschwitz," said director Stephan Suschke before the premiere. "But I still hope they will be able to sympathise with her so it won't be so easy to distance themselves from her."
But the play drew vitriol from Berlin's hardened critics.

"Do we really need conjecture today about the emotional life of a woman who had no importance except as the girlfriend of a mass murderer?" asked Info Radio's theatre critic. "The play is basically banal and fundamentally tasteless."

"The monologue is neither funny nor startling, illuminating nor irritating," wrote the Berliner Morgenpost. "It doesn't attempt to show the indefinable figure behind the stuffed bra or the real story behind the doomed bunker."

The monologue covers Braun's fear of her impending suicide, dreams of paparazzi toasting her as a Hollywood heroine in 1990s Berlin and her imagined screenplay of "the world's greatest love story" in which Clark Gable plays the Fuehrer.
Advertisements and media coverage inundated the city during the week before the premiere. A menacing male voice warned radio listeners in English that "Eva Braun is back in town".
Harfouch, born in East Germany, is a star in demand for German film and television as well as the stage and has received near-unanimous rave reviews in a flurry of recent appearances.
But even the usually unabashed Bild tabloid suggested that the risque "Eva" material might prove "the flop of her life".
Loud boos accompanied applause when she took her final bow but Harfouch was undaunted.
"I found the audience's reaction appropriate," she said.
"I myself swing between nausea, cloying emotion and love with this role, and then sometimes feel completely distant from it. If the audience were also ambivalent, I'm satisfied."
